stem: ‘Textiles have such an important bearing on our daily lives.’ (www.coats.com)

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — no 4, so a bare statement drops to 3. Silk comes from the cocoon of the silkworm. The scheme lists the stages in order, so write the process as a sequence and the 5 is safe.

options: silkworms eat leaves of mulberry tree

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Single-word properties, so give several and say what each means for wearing or washing the fabric — a list of adjectives alone reads as one thin point.

rows.verbatim: Test to identify a natural fibre
rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. This is the burn test and the first two options are the method itself — hold the fabric over a flameproof dish and ignite it. The marks then come from what you observe for this fibre: how it takes the flame, the residue, and the smell.

options: hold fabric over a flame proof dish
sizzles and curls away from the flame
leaves a dark bead which can be crushed
leaves ash that is a dark, gritty, fine powder
gives out little or no smoke

notes: One of four parallel profiles the scheme prints under Q2(b). A candidate profiles a single fibre, so each fibre is its own card with its own questionRef rather than pooling four sets of marking points into one menu. The test row keeps the scheme's shared method lines ahead of the fibre-specific observations.

questionText: Describe two fashion trends currently popular in summer clothing.
stem: ‘Fashion has two purposes comfort and love.’ (Coco Chanel)

rows.verbatim: Fashion trends currently popular in summer clothing
rows.contextNote: Only two points at 3 marks — a six-mark part. Describe, so name the garment and say what makes it the trend: the cut, the fabric, or the finish.

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss three factors that influence a person’s choice when choosing work wear clothing.
stem: ‘Fashion has two purposes comfort and love.’ (Coco Chanel)

rows.verbatim: Factors influencing the choice of work wear clothing
rows.contextNote: Three factors at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. Tie each to the job — high visibility and waterproofing matter for outdoor work, easy care and ease of movement for a busy indoor job. A factor named without the job it suits is 2.

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Explain the following types of work: paid work; unpaid work; voluntary work.
stem: ‘Of women over 15 years of age in Ireland, more than 50% of them are in the workforce.’ (www.cso.ie)

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — the longest of the three lists. Beyond "done for money", the scheme credits the forms it takes (permanent, temporary, full-time, part-time, contract) and the security it brings (pension, PRSI, holiday and sick pay).

options: may be permanent, temporary, full-time, part-time or contract based
self-employed or employed by another person
can be completed from home setting or designated work setting
a wide range of skills required from manual to managerial positions
provides security in the form of pension, PRSI, holiday and sick pay

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Unpaid work is still work — childrearing, caring for older or disabled family members, housework, DIY, and work placement. Name examples, do not just say it is unpaid.

options: domestic housework i.e. child rearing, caring for elderly/disabled

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The shortest list, so it needs all of it: for a community or charity, no financial reward, and done to make a difference to other people.

options: involves working for community or for a charity
helping other people and making a difference in other peoples’ lives

notes: Fixed: three named types of work, priced identically. The distinction between unpaid and voluntary is the one students blur — unpaid work is for your own household, voluntary work is for someone else's.

questionText: Discuss three reasons for the increased participation of women in the work force.
stem: ‘Of women over 15 years of age in Ireland, more than 50% of them are in the workforce.’ (www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Reasons for the increased participation of women in the workforce
rows.contextNote: Three reasons at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — no 4, so a reason without development drops to 3. The list has two halves: what changed for women (better educated, equal pay, equality legislation) and what changed at home (childcare options, flexible hours, two incomes needed). One from each shows range.

options: better working conditions, e.g. job share, flexitime, career breaks
greater variety of childcare options available
two incomes needed to meet high cost of living

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Evaluate the impact of dual earner families on family life.
stem: ‘Of women over 15 years of age in Ireland, more than 50% of them are in the workforce.’ (www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Impact of dual earner families on family life
rows.contextNote: Four points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — the biggest single row in the elective. Evaluate means both directions score: higher income and both parents sharing the childrearing, but also role overload, role conflict, and children who feel neglected. An answer that is all positive leaves marks behind.

options: both parents involved in child rearing
both parents involved in household tasks
children have better attitude towards work

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss how family leisure activities are influenced by each of the following: gender; age; cultural influences.
stem: Leisure time is time that a person is free from work or other duties.

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Two angles: some activities are still male or female dominated, and whoever works outside the home has less leisure time.

options: women/men working outside the home have less time for leisure

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — the richest of the three lists. The scheme walks the life cycle: young people have time but little money, parents of small children have neither, retired couples have both, older people have time but physical limits.

options: young people have fewer commitments and more time for leisure
couples with young children have the least amount of time and disposable income
retired couples have more time and money to spend on leisure
older people have less money, may have physical constraints and do more sedentary pursuits
some leisure activities are regarded as too dangerous for children e.g. under 10’s may not scuba dive

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Culture here means place and tradition — surfing or hurling tied to a particular county, Irish music tied to the country, and children copying their parents' activities.

options: in a particular area of a county, e.g. surfing, hurling
traditional to a country, e.g. Irish music
children’s choice of leisure activities often influenced by parent’s activities

notes: Fixed: three named influences, priced identically. Skipping one costs a straight 5.

questionText: Evaluate the benefits of participating in leisure activities for family members.
stem: Leisure time is time that a person is free from work or other duties.

rows.verbatim: Benefits of participating in leisure activities
rows.contextNote: Three benefits at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme covers physical, mental, social and family benefits — taking one from different areas reads as three genuine benefits rather than one restated. Say who benefits and how.

options: helps relax and unwind from stresses of daily life
assist the development of new skills

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Evaluate the impact of the following on family life: improvements in the provision of education; parenting roles within the family; improved conditions at work.
stem: Social and economic changes have impacted on family life in Ireland today.

rows.verbatim: improvements in the provision of education
rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The named schemes are the marks — SUSI, HEAR, DARE, VTOS, PLC and SOLAS courses. Say what each opened up for families who could not afford it before.

options: special classes for pupils with additional needs
SNA’s at primary and secondary level
abolition of fees, SUSI grants, HEAR, DARE have made third level education more accessible
PLC courses and SOLAS training programmes

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — the longest list. The change is the point: both parents working, fathers at home, women as breadwinners, an egalitarian split of childcare, and the role conflict and overload that came with it.

options: parents discipline their children so that they learn to behave in an acceptable manner within society
cultural values or religious beliefs are passed onto children
both parents work outside the home and children go to creche
men staying at home to mind children
children have greater say in family matters
egalitarian approach to childcare and household tasks

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Shorter hours, better pay, more disposable income, safer workplaces — and the scheme explicitly credits the knock-on that happier workers make for better family life.

options: more disposable income and a higher standard of living
people are happier at work which can have a positive effect on family life
health and safety regulations ensure a safer work environment

notes: Fixed: three named changes, priced identically.

questionText: Describe how second-level education prepares students for participation in the workplace.
stem: Social and economic changes have impacted on family life in Ireland today.

rows.verbatim: How second-level education prepares students for the workplace
rows.contextNote: Three points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The list splits into skills (literacy, numeracy, computer) and qualities (punctuality, responsibility, respect for authority, self-discipline). Take from both, and say how school builds each one.

options: develop qualities, e.g. respect for authority

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Give an account of the nutritive value and the dietetic value of milk.
stem: ‘Your body needs lots of different nutrients to stay healthy.’ (www.safefood.net)

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, on a 5:4:3:2:0 ladder — partial credit is real, so write what you know. Nutritive value is which nutrients are present and how much: HBV protein, saturated fat, lactose, calcium, 87% water. The two deficiencies, vitamin C and iron, are marking points too.

options: carbohydrates in the form of lactose
traces of magnesium, potassium and sodium
deficient in Vitamin C and iron

rows.contextNote: One point, 5 marks, 5:4:3:2:0. Dietetic value is who it suits and why — easy to digest, inexpensive, versatile in sweet and savoury dishes, important for children, adolescents, pregnant women and older people. This is the half students merge into the first and lose.

options: HBV protein for growth and repair
saturated fat, provides heat and energy
carbohydrate in form of lactose for energy
calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth
important for children, adolescents, pregnant women and elderly
used in both sweet and savoury dishes
can be fortified with vitamins and minerals
should be combined with foods rich in starch, fibre, iron to have balance in the diet
wide range of different types available to suit different diets, tastes and requirements

rows.verbatim: Two further points, from either heading
rows.contextNote: The scheme reads "1 reference to nutritive value, 1 reference to dietetic value, & 2 other points", so half the marks float.

options: carbohydrates in the form of lactose
traces of magnesium, potassium and sodium
deficient in Vitamin C and iron
HBV protein for growth and repair
saturated fat, provides heat and energy
carbohydrate in form of lactose for energy
calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth
important for children, adolescents, pregnant women and elderly

notes: Fixed: one point pinned to each named value and two floating. Nutritive is what is in it; dietetic is who it suits.

questionText: Outline three different ways that dairy foods can be included as part of a healthy diet.
stem: ‘Your body needs lots of different nutrients to stay healthy.’ (www.safefood.net)

rows.verbatim: Ways dairy foods can be included in a healthy diet
rows.contextNote: Three ways at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The question says different, so take three different dairy foods rather than three uses of milk. Naming the food is 2 — the other 2 come from the dish you put it in.

options: Milk, milk with cereal; part of milkshake/smoothie, glass of milk with a meal; added to scrambled eggs; in white sauce for cauliflower, over bacon, in pasta bakes, lasagnes; added to mashed potatoes
Cheese, grilled cheese sandwich; crackers and cheese; part of salads; added to scrambled eggs; garnish for soups
Yoghurt, instead of milk with cereals; part of smoothies; a snack; added to curries; part of a dip
Cream, garnish for soups; added to mashed potatoes; used in white sauces; accompaniment to desserts; served with scones

questionText: Discuss three factors that should be considered when choosing a kitchen appliance.
stem: ‘Choosing an electrical appliance, less is usually best.’ (www.electricireland.com)

rows.verbatim: Factors to consider when choosing a kitchen appliance
rows.contextNote: Three factors at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — no 4, so a factor named without a reason drops to 3. The list runs from the appliance itself (cost, energy rating, size, function, guarantee) to how you found out about it (consumer websites, leaflets, word of mouth), and both halves score.

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Describe three guidelines to follow for the safe use of electrical kitchen appliances.
stem: ‘Choosing an electrical appliance, less is usually best.’ (www.electricireland.com)

rows.verbatim: Guidelines for the safe use of electrical kitchen appliances
rows.contextNote: Three guidelines at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Describe, so say what each one prevents — wet hands conduct electricity, a trailing flex over a hob can melt, an overloaded socket can catch fire. The danger is where the marks are.

options: buy appliances with a safety approval mark
ensure plugs are correctly wired and replace if defective
examine flexes for wear and tear
do not handle sockets, plugs or electrical appliances with wet hands
do not have flexes trailing over hob or sink
do not use adapters/extension leads to overload sockets

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Outline conditions necessary for a marriage to be legally valid in Ireland.
stem: ‘There was a total of 23,173 marriages celebrated in Ireland in 2022.’ (www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Conditions for a marriage to be legally valid in Ireland
rows.contextNote: Three conditions at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The two numbers are the reliable marks — three months' notice to the registrar, and both parties over 18. Free to marry, not closely related, and two witnesses present are the other safe ones.

options: three months’ notice required by registrar
partners must be over 18 years of age
both people must be free to marry, cannot be married already
partners must not be too closely related
the register must be signed by the couple and witnesses
all marriages must be registered after the ceremony
must take place in a registered building, e.g. registry office, church, or approved venue

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss three responsibilities of a couple within a marriage relationship.
stem: ‘There was a total of 23,173 marriages celebrated in Ireland in 2022.’ (www.cso.ie)

rows.verbatim: Responsibilities of a couple within a marriage relationship
rows.contextNote: Three responsibilities at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — the shortest list on the paper, so all five options are worth knowing. The legal duty to provide for the physical, emotional, social, moral and educational needs of the children is the one that develops most easily to a full 5.

options: provide financial support for partner and children
legal duty to provide for the physical, emotional, social, moral and educational needs of the children
work on the relationship to ensure it is functioning

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Describe the factors that influence interior design in the home. Refer to: aesthetic and comfort factors; environmental awareness.
stem: ‘Ireland’s Better Energy Warmer Homes scheme aims to help individuals make their homes warmer, healthier and cheaper to run.’ (www.seai.ie)

rows.contextNote: Two points at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0 — the longer of the two lists, covering both halves of the heading: how a room looks (elements and principles of design, personal taste, trends) and how it works to live in (comfort, heating, lighting, ergonomics).

options: use of trends that will date easily/ quickly
suitable for individuals with disabilities who are sedentary
zoned heating to provide different temperatures/variety of levels of heat

rows.contextNote: Two points at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The scheme runs the whole product life cycle — making it, using it, disposing of it — plus where the materials came from. Reuse, recycle and repurpose are three separate options.

options: impact of materials used on the environment

rows.verbatim: One further point, from either heading
rows.contextNote: The scheme reads "2 points on each heading + 1 other", so the fifth point floats.

options: use of trends that will date easily/ quickly
suitable for individuals with disabilities who are sedentary
zoned heating to provide different temperatures/variety of levels of heat

notes: Fixed: two points pinned to each named heading and the fifth floating. Ignoring a heading caps you at 12 of 20.

questionText: Discuss levels of thermal comfort in relation to two different living spaces in the home.
stem: ‘Ireland’s Better Energy Warmer Homes scheme aims to help individuals make their homes warmer, healthier and cheaper to run.’ (www.seai.ie)

tariffModel.notation: 2 points @ 6 marks: identify room @ 2 marks (graded 2:0), discussion @ 4 marks (graded 4:2:0), x2

rows.contextNote: Two rooms named, 2 marks each, graded 2:0 — all-or-nothing and almost free. Name them before you discuss anything.

rows.verbatim: Thermal comfort in the rooms identified
rows.contextNote: Two discussions at 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. The temperature ranges are the marks and they differ sharply by room — living rooms 17–21°C, bedrooms 10–16°C, kitchens 15–19°C, bathrooms 16–19°C. Quote the range and say why the room needs it. A minimum of 20°C is recommended for older people whatever the room.

options: depends on room function e.g. sitting or carrying out light work 19°C to 23°C
recommended temperature for living rooms is 17°C to 21°C
minimum temperature of 20°C is recommended for elderly people

notes: Fixed: the scheme prices naming the room separately from discussing it, twice over, so the card splits them into a naming row and a discussion row.

questionText: Explain the underlying principle of a thermostat and describe how it can be used in the home.
stem: ‘Ireland’s Better Energy Warmer Homes scheme aims to help individuals make their homes warmer, healthier and cheaper to run.’ (www.seai.ie)

tariffModel.notation: Underlying principle 4 points @ 3 marks; use in the home 2 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0)

rows.contextNote: Four points at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0 — twelve of the eighteen marks. The scheme wants the bimetal strip in sequence: two metals, brass expands readily and invar barely, so the strip bends on heating, which breaks the circuit and switches the appliance off, and it straightens on cooling to switch it back on. That chain is four points on its own.

options: based on the principle of thermal expansion
contain a bimetal strip, composed of two metals
invar expands only slightly when heated
when heat is applied the brass expands and the strip bends
this breaks the electrical circuit and switches off the appliance
on cooling the bimetallic strip returns to its original shape switching on the appliance again

rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. Ten appliances are accepted, so this half should never be lost — name the appliance and say what the thermostat holds steady in it.

notes: Fixed: the principle is priced at 12 and the uses at 6, so two thirds of the marks are in the physics.

questionText: Explain the underlying principle of one type of energy-efficient lighting.
stem: ‘Lighting ideas are an essential part of space design.’ (www.homesandgardens.com)

tariffModel.notation: Name 4 marks (graded 4:2:0); underlying principle 2 points @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0)

rows.contextNote: Name one, 4 marks, graded 4:2:0. Only two are accepted, and the CFL has by far the longer explanation in the scheme — name that one unless you are confident on the LED semiconductor account.

rows.verbatim: Underlying principle of the type named
rows.contextNote: Two points at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. For the CFL the chain is: a phosphor-coated tube holding argon and mercury, electrodes heat up and vaporise the mercury, the gas reacts with the phosphor and it glows. For the LED it is electroluminescence — electrons combine with holes and release photons.

options: lights made compact by looping the tube a number of times
consists of a glass tube coated with phosphor
when electricity flows electrodes at each end of the glass tube heat up causing mercury to vaporise
the gases react with the phosphor coating and cause it to glow
when switched on electrodes combine with holes within the bulb releasing energy (photons)
the colour is determined by the energy band gap of the semi-conductor

notes: Fixed: the name is priced at 4 and the principle at 6. The principle row pools both accepted types, because the two points are awarded for whichever was named.

questionText: Discuss how environmental, economic and social factors influence the choice of housing styles in Ireland today.

rows.contextNote: One point, 6 marks, on a 6:4:2:0 ladder — a developed paragraph, not a phrase. Energy efficiency, the aspect of the site, local materials, climate and building regulations.
One point, 6 marks, 6:4:2:0. The longest list: income, site cost, size and style, materials, bills, and the resale or investment value.
One point, 6 marks, 6:4:2:0. Personal taste, location, what the family needs, a member with special needs, and local tradition.

notes: Fixed: the scheme expects one point on each named factor, so all three must be attempted. Missing one costs a straight 6.

questionText: Describe the impact of burning fossil fuels in the home. Refer to: an emission produced by burning fossil fuels; effects on the environment; a strategy households could implement in order to reduce emissions.
stem: ‘We have been forced to rethink how we live in our homes in recent years.’ (The Irish Times)

tariffModel.notation: Emission 1 @ 3 marks (graded 3:0); effects 2 points @ 3 marks; strategy 1 point @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0)

rows.verbatim: An emission produced by burning fossil fuels
rows.contextNote: Name one emission, 3 marks, graded 3:0 — all-or-nothing, and naming a second adds nothing. Six are accepted, so this is three free marks.

Two effects at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. The scheme goes past "climate change" to the consequences — rising sea levels, damage to crops, spread of infectious disease, shifting plant and animal ranges. Naming the effect is 2; saying what it does is 3.

options: changes in distribution of plant and animal species

rows.contextNote: One strategy, 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. It must be something a household can actually do — switch to renewables or smokeless fuel, fit timers and thermostats, stop burning rubbish.

options: choose natural gas instead of oil
use timers and thermostats on heating systems

notes: Fixed: three headings named in the question, priced 3 / 6 / 3.

questionText: Sketch and describe an outfit to wear for your graduation ball.
stem: A special occasion is an opportunity for an individual to showcase their unique sense of style.

rows.contextNote: Six marks for the drawing, on a 6:4:2:0 ladder — half the part. The scheme wants design features visible and labelled: line, shape, proportion and harmony. Label the sketch; an unlabelled drawing cannot show the examiner you knew what you were doing.

options: should show detail of design features i.e. line, shape, proportion, harmony

rows.contextNote: Three points at 2 marks, graded 2:1:0 — short items, not sentences. Twelve features are accepted, so pick three that are actually visible in your sketch.

notes: Fixed: the sketch is priced at 6 and the description at 6. The sketch is the candidate's own drawing, so unlike the outfit-evaluation questions on other papers this needs no figure from the exam paper.

questionText: Suggest a suitable fabric for the outfit and give a reason for your answer.
stem: A special occasion is an opportunity for an individual to showcase their unique sense of style.

rows.contextNote: Name one fabric, 3 marks, graded 3:0 — all-or-nothing. Seven are accepted.

questionText: Evaluate the socio-economic factors that impact household expenditure.
stem: Everyday living includes many transactions that require consumer spending.

rows.contextNote: Three factors at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 — no 4, so a factor named without its effect on spending drops to 3. The scheme prints five factors; take three different ones rather than three angles on income. Social class and culture have the most developed accounts.

options: mortgage payments; families with young children require childcare; school expenses; older people have mortgage paid
women in workforce; dual income families; more disposable income

some from poorer background leave school earlier without qualifications; may lead to unemployment, dependence on social welfare payments; middle class backgrounds generally better educational opportunities, more likely to gain qualifications leading to better paid jobs and more discretionary spending

cultures focus more on providing for needs; more affluent cultures spend more on luxuries, more disposable income; some cultures restrict women for working outside the home which impacts on money available for spending

notes: One option per named factor, each carrying that factor's own account, because the scheme groups its marking points under five headings and prices three points.

stem: Everyday living includes many transactions that require consumer spending.

options: back to school clothing and footwear allowance
provision of grants for third level students

questionText: Evaluate the contribution of the microwave oven to the management of the home.
stem: ‘Irish people are cooking more at home, and how we shop for food, cook and eat has changed significantly.’ (The Irish Times)

rows.verbatim: Contribution of the microwave oven to home management
rows.contextNote: Three points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Management is the key word — these are savings of time, energy, skill and washing-up, so tie each point to the resource it saves the household.

options: safe to use by children and/elderly
food can be cooked and served in same dish

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Describe the working principle of the microwave oven.
stem: ‘Irish people are cooking more at home, and how we shop for food, cook and eat has changed significantly.’ (The Irish Times)

rows.verbatim: Working principle of the microwave oven
rows.contextNote: Five points at 3 marks, graded 3:2:0. The scheme lists the chain in order and following it gives five points without effort: the transformer raises the voltage, the magnetron turns electricity into electromagnetic waves, the wave-guide directs them into the cabinet, they penetrate 2–4 cm and vibrate the food molecules, and the friction produces heat that conducts to the centre. Standing time is a marking point because the molecules keep vibrating after the timer stops.

options: magnetron changes electrical energy to electromagnetic energy
wave-guide guides the microwaves into cabinet
microwaves penetrate food to a depth of 2-4 cm
microwaves cause food molecules to vibrate rapidly
causes friction and produces high heat
heat spreads to the centre of food through conduction
allow standing time as the molecules continue to vibrate after cooking time
incorporated grill browns food by radiation

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss three factors which should be considered when choosing a heating system for the home.
stem: A contemporary bathroom design is shown below.

rows.verbatim: Factors to consider when choosing a heating system
rows.contextNote: Three factors at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 - no 4, so a factor named without a reason drops to 3. The scheme prints eight factors, so take three genuinely different ones: cost, how it is controlled, and what it does to the environment.

options: automatic timer that is easy to use; thermostat to control heating; smart technology
priority for family with young children
immersion with a timer to save electricity; instantaneous heaters
gas and smokeless fuel produce less pollution

notes: One option per named factor, each carrying that factor's own detail, because the scheme groups its marking points under eight headings and prices three.

questionText: Describe three guidelines to follow for the safe use of electricity in the home.

rows.verbatim: Guidelines for the safe use of electricity in the home
rows.contextNote: Three guidelines at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Describe, so say what each one prevents - water conducts electricity, a flex across a hob can melt, an overloaded adaptor can catch fire. The danger is where the extra marks are.

options: do not use electrical appliances in the bathroom except shaver sockets
use pull cords for light switches
purchase only electrical appliances that carry recognised safety symbols
avoid overuse of adaptors and extension cables
check electric blankets for sign of wear
do not pull flexes across cooker hob or sink
always read and follow manufacturer’s instructions
keep electric heaters away from curtains

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Describe three strategies that could be used to improve energy efficiency in the home.
stem: ‘A quarter of all energy used in Ireland is consumed directly in homes.’ (www.seai.ie)

rows.verbatim: Strategies to improve energy efficiency in the home
rows.contextNote: Three strategies at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Spread them - one on keeping heat in, one on heating water, one on appliances - so they cannot be read as the same strategy three times. Say how each saves the energy.

options: turn off lights when not in use
have timer and thermostat on immersion
do not leave appliances on stand-by

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Name one renewable energy source and outline the advantages of the energy source named.
stem: ‘A quarter of all energy used in Ireland is consumed directly in homes.’ (www.seai.ie)

rows.contextNote: Name one, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Six are accepted, but solar has by far the most detailed list of advantages in the scheme - name that one unless you know another well, because the other 10 marks depend on it.

rows.verbatim: Advantages of the energy source named
rows.contextNote: Two advantages at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0 - ten of the fifteen marks. The strongest answers pair a money advantage with an environmental one: solar saves up to 68% on heating bills and raises the BER, and it produces no carbon dioxide. Grants are a marking point in their own right.

options: saves up to 68% on heating bills
plentiful supply of hot water for space and water heating
converts light from sun directly into electricity
increasing the property value by raising the BER
very viable to operate in Ireland
running costs once the plant is set up are low

notes: Fixed: naming is priced at 5 and the advantages at 10. The advantages row pools all six sources, because the two points are awarded for whichever was named.

questionText: Describe the function of the following parts of a cold-water supply to a house: stop cock; storage tank; overflow pipe.

rows.contextNote: One function, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Say where it is as well as what it does - on the service pipe outside or under the kitchen sink - and that it shuts the supply off if there is a problem.

options: special valve found on a service pipe outside the house/under the kitchen sink
allows the water supply to be shut off if there is a problem

rows.contextNote: One function, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The height is the point: it sits in the attic so gravity gives the pressure to feed the toilet, shower and hot press below.

options: located in the attic at elevated level
improves pressure to supply the system
a ball valve controls the level of water in the tank
stores the cold water which supplies the cold-water to toilet, shower and hot press tank

rows.contextNote: One function, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. It carries excess water outside, and the scheme wants the reason it is needed - if the ball valve fails, it stops the house flooding.

options: attic storage tanks are fitted with an overflow pipe leading to the outside of the house and carries excess water out of the house
if the ball valve fails to work it prevents flooding

notes: Fixed: three named parts, priced identically. All three are short and factual.

questionText: Outline three guidelines to follow to reduce water usage in the home.

rows.verbatim: Guidelines to reduce water usage in the home
rows.contextNote: Three guidelines at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme groups its tips by where the water is used - toilet, taps, appliances, washing - so taking one from different groups gives three that are genuinely different. Say how much each saves or why it works.

options: install a dual flush toilet; a rainwater harvesting system linked to the water system can be used to flush toilets
repair leaking taps; do not wash items under a running tap; do not leave taps running while washing teeth; use a basin in the sink rather than washing under a running tap
fill kettle with the amount of water needed; wait until the washing machine or dishwasher is full before turning on; use economy or eco wash cycle
use a shower instead of a bath

notes: One option per place water is used, each carrying that group's own tips, because three guidelines drawn from one group would read as one guideline restated.

questionText: Name and describe one fabric finish. Give an example of its use in clothing.

tariffModel.notation: Name 4 marks (graded 4:2:0); description 1 point @ 3 marks (graded 3:2:0); example 1 point @ 2 marks (graded 2:0)

One description, 3 marks, graded 3:2:0, matching the finish you named. Each of the scheme's descriptions is a single clause about what the fabric can now do - that is the whole answer.

options: prevents fabric from clinging to the skin
makes fabrics easier to clean and keep clean
prevents fabrics from creasing, reducing the need for ironing
makes the fabric stronger and more absorbent

mortgage arrears, homelessness, reposition of homes
lack of money can prevent participation in leisure and social activities
loss of purpose and sense of direction

provision of basic needs may be difficult
families may become homeless or in need of emergency accommodation
children may be unable to attend college due to lack of money

increase in the black economy to supplement welfare allowance

options: develop qualities e.g. respect for authority

options: playing with toys helps with manual dexterity e.g. jigsaws; practical subjects can improve fine and gross motor skills; development of hand/eye co-ordination; sport and physical education helps to build healthy bones/muscles and improve balance/fitness
young children gain emotional independence from parents, encourages maturity; feelings for themselves and others; learn to be sensitive to needs of others; supportive of others; expressing emotions

promoted through the wide range of subjects; extracurricular activities; classmates encourage competition; examinations provide challenges; resources e.g. books, computers assist development; provides stimulation and nurtures a learning environment; support for children with ALN’s

peers, can be positive or negative
school environment e.g. resources in school
access to computers/assistive technology, reader pens

questionText: Discuss the impact of social and economic changes on family life. Refer to: reduction in working hours; increased participation of women in the workforce; equal pay and employment opportunities.

options: better work and family life balance
more time to spend with families
parents can collect children from school
increase in physical activities resulting from more leisure time

dual income contributes to a higher standard of living
children spend more time in childcare
may lead to stress, role conflict
teenagers become more responsible and share household chores
working mothers can be a positive role model for children

questionText: Outline three benefits of voluntary work to the community.
stem: Ireland has undergone many social and economic changes in the past 20 years.

options: can provide a quick service e.g. care of the elderly
friendships and bonds can be formed
creates a sense of community spirit
provides new skills in an area
complements work carried out by statutory bodies
offers a more personal local service

questionText: Give an account of the causes of osteoporosis and the effects of osteoporosis on the body.
stem: ‘It is estimated that up to 300,000 people in Ireland have osteoporosis.’ (www.irishosteoporosis.ie)

tariffModel.notation: 4 points @ 5 marks (graded 5:3:0) (1 cause, 1 effect, plus 2 others)

rows.contextNote: One cause, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The scheme is explicit that at least one cause is required. Calcium and vitamin D lead the list, but low oestrogen after menopause is the one that explains why the condition is far more common in women.

options: lack of calcium rich foods in the diet from an early age
low levels of oestrogen in postmenopausal women
medications e.g. for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis

rows.verbatim: One effect of osteoporosis on the body
rows.contextNote: One effect, 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. At least one effect is required. "Brittle bones" is the definition rather than an effect - fractures, loss of height, a curved spine and back pain are what the examiner is after.

rows.verbatim: Two further points, from either causes or effects
rows.contextNote: Two further points at 5 marks each, and the scheme lets these come from either list - "1 cause, 1 effect, plus 2 others". So two more causes, two more effects, or one of each all score.

options: lack of calcium rich foods in the diet from an early age
low levels of oestrogen in postmenopausal women
medications e.g. for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis

notes: Fixed: the scheme requires one cause and one effect, then floats the remaining 10 marks across both lists. Modelled as three rows so the two compulsory points cannot be lost.

questionText: Evaluate three lifestyle and/or dietary guidelines to follow in order to prevent osteoporosis.
stem: ‘It is estimated that up to 300,000 people in Ireland have osteoporosis.’ (www.irishosteoporosis.ie)

rows.verbatim: Lifestyle and/or dietary guidelines to prevent osteoporosis
rows.contextNote: Three guidelines at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. "And/or" means all three may come from one list, so you are not forced to balance them. Evaluate, so say why it works - weight-bearing exercise loads the bone and builds density; sunshine is where the vitamin D comes from.

options: take calcium and vitamin D supplements
balance protein intake, too much or too little can have an effect on bone density
avoid calcium absorption inhibitors, e.g. excessive fibre, tannins

notes: One flat list pooling the lifestyle and dietary clusters, because the question prices them together and the scheme accepts either.

questionText: Discuss the role of food labelling as a source of consumer information for people following a special diet.
stem: ‘It is estimated that up to 300,000 people in Ireland have osteoporosis.’ (www.irishosteoporosis.ie)

rows.verbatim: Role of food labelling for people following a special diet
rows.contextNote: Three roles at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. Tie each one back to the special diet - the allergen list is the strongest, because for a coeliac or a nut allergy it is the difference between safe and dangerous. Nutrient panels serve the diabetic and the low-salt diet.

options: helps consumer make an informed decision about purchasing foods
informs consumer on information on nutrients, people opt for more nutritious alternatives
allergens listed reduces the risk of suffering an allergic reaction
ingredients listed in descending order of weight
help to choose the more nutritional options
quality assurance e.g. Bord Bia mark

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Identify and explain three factors that affect household income.

equal pay for all, some managerial positions still male dominated

some students from lower socio-economic backgrounds leave school early without qualifications, may lead to unemployment; middle class backgrounds generally better educational opportunities, more likely to gain qualifications leading to better paid jobs
different cultures value income differently; some cultures determine whether women can work outside the home

notes: One option per named factor, each carrying that factor's own detail, because the scheme groups its marking points under five headings and prices three.

questionText: Describe three benefits of setting up a family budget plan.
stem: Money management is an important life skill.

options: alleviates worry and stress as bills will be paid
know where all monies are going
encourages people to wait until they have the money to buy something

notes: One flat list, taken in order to the cap.

questionText: Discuss how the role of the adolescent has changed in the modern family.

rows.verbatim: How the role of the adolescent has changed
rows.contextNote: Three points at 5 marks, graded 5:3:0. The word is "changed", so each point works best as a contrast with the past - adolescents now share in decisions, mind siblings, cook meals and hold part-time jobs where once they did not.

options: more input into family decision making

questionText: Explain how the family supports the physical and emotional development of children.

options: provides basic needs e.g. food, clothes, shelter
protects vulnerable members by providing a safe environment
provides a safe and secure place to discuss feelings
help children to develop good self- esteem

questionText: Comment on the suitability of the occasion wear shown above. Refer to: shape; comfort; design features.

questionRef: 2023 HL Section B Q2(a) — Deferred sitting
questionText: Write an informative account of coeliac disease. Refer to: • causes and symptoms • specific dietary guidelines a coeliac should follow.
stem: ‘Research reveals that up to one in every 100 people have coeliac disease and many more have an intolerance to gluten.’ (www.safefood.net)

rows.contextNote: Two cause points, each graded 4:2:0. Source clarification (ESPGHAN, 2024): introduction of gluten between completed four and twelve months has not been shown to change cumulative coeliac-disease incidence. The before-six-months statement below is historical examination wording. Published 2023 scheme guidance: coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition, the immune system fights healthy cells in the body instead of bacteria or viruses; body's immune system has an abnormal reaction to gluten in the diet, present in foods such as bread, pasta, cereals and biscuits; the immune system mistakes gluten as a threat to the body and produces antibodies that attack parts of the body that are healthy; small intestine becomes red and swollen; the villi foldings flatten in the small intestine; this reduces the ability of the body to absorb nutrients and deficiency such as anaemia can occur; family history may increase the risk of coeliac disease; gluten in a baby’s diet before 6 months may increase the risk of coeliac disease etc.

Three symptoms, each graded 2:0. Published guidance: abdominal pain; bloating and flatulence; indigestion; constipation; vomiting; unexpected weight loss; an itchy rash; tingling and numbness in hands and feet; disorders that affect coordination, balance and speech (ataxia); swelling of the hands, feet, arms and legs caused by a build-up of fluid (oedema); extreme tiredness etc.

Two dietary points, each graded 4:2:0. Source clarification (HSE): ordinary oats can be contaminated; most people with coeliac disease tolerate avenin, but some react. HSE advises discussing oats with a dietitian. The broad “avoid oats” wording below is retained as 2023 marking guidance. Published guidance: choose gluten free foods; select products with the gluten free symbol; read labels carefully for hidden gluten in products; avoid foods containing gluten – wheat, oats, barley, rye and their products; choose rice and corn and their products; consume naturally gluten free products, e.g. vegetables, fruit, meat, eggs, nuts and seeds etc.

questionRef: 2023 HL Section B Q3(a) — Deferred sitting
questionText: Set out details of one method of home food preservation that involves the application of heat. Refer to: • name • how the method of preservation is carried out • the underlying principle.
stem: Food preservation helps to reduce food waste and to increase the availability of different foods.

rows.contextNote: Name the method you describe, graded 2:0. Published example: Jam/chutney making

Five method points, each graded 2:1:0. Published examination outline (recipe-specific processing times are not supplied): weigh out ingredients accurately; wash jars in hot, soapy water and dry; place on a baking tray and sterilise in the oven at 140°C for 20 minutes to remove microbes; remove bruised or damaged fruit; wash, peel, remove stalks and leaves and cut evenly; place fruit/vegetables in a greased saucepan and simmer gently to soften and release pectin from the cell walls; some fruits require the addition of water; warm sugar in the oven at 140°C for five minutes to help it dissolve quicker, reducing the risk of crystallisation; add the sugar to the fruit and stir until it is fully dissolved; addition of vinegar; bring to the boil and boil rapidly, stirring occasionally; check if the jam has reached its setting point; if jam is set, skim the scum from the top; using a ladle, spoon into the sterilised jars, leaving 1.5 cm head space at the top; cover with a wax disc; removing any air bubbles with the back of a spoon; apply a cellophane cover over the top of the jar to form an airtight seal; hold the cellophane cover in place with an elastic band; place a lid on top; label the jar with the date of potting and type of jam; store in a cool, dry place.

Three principle points, each graded 4:2:0. Published guidance: high heat is used to soften the fruit and to kill microbes and enzymes; high proportion of sugar is used to help setting and acts as a preservative; sugar dissolves in the water of the fruit forming a concentrated solution; water is then drawn from any microbial cells by osmosis to equalise the solution; this dehydrates the microbial cells causing death; good quality, ripe fruit will have a high pectin content which will help setting; acid is necessary to draw pectin out of the fruit, giving a better colour and flavour and helps to prevent crystallisation; lemons are added if the fruit does not have a high acid content; ripe fruit has adequate pectin present; some fruits have more pectin than others, so fruits are often combined to maintain pectin content; sealing prevents the re-entry of micro-organisms; sterilising – to kill bacteria present; pH – the vinegar in chutney lowers the pH which prevents microbial growth;

Published examination outline (recipe-specific processing times are not supplied): weigh out ingredients accurately; wash jars in hot, soapy water and dry; place on a baking tray and sterilise in the oven at 140°C for 20 minutes to remove microbes; remove bruised or damaged fruit; wash, peel, remove stalks and leaves and cut evenly; place fruit/vegetables in a greased saucepan and simmer gently to soften and release pectin from the cell walls; some fruits require the addition of water; warm sugar in the oven at 140°C for five minutes to help it dissolve quicker, reducing the risk of crystallisation; add the sugar to the fruit and stir until it is fully dissolved; addition of vinegar; bring to the boil and boil rapidly, stirring occasionally; check if the jam has reached its setting point; if jam is set, skim the scum from the top; using a ladle, spoon into the sterilised jars, leaving 1.5 cm head space at the top; cover with a wax disc; removing any air bubbles with the back of a spoon; apply a cellophane cover over the top of the jar to form an airtight seal; hold the cellophane cover in place with an elastic band; place a lid on top; label the jar with the date of potting and type of jam; store in a cool, dry place.

Three principle points, each graded 4:2:0. Published guidance: high heat is used to soften the fruit and to kill microbes and enzymes; high proportion of sugar is used to help setting and acts as a preservative; sugar dissolves in the water of the fruit forming a concentrated solution; water is then drawn from any microbial cells by osmosis to equalise the solution; this dehydrates the microbial cells causing death; good quality, ripe fruit will have a high pectin content which will help setting; acid is necessary to draw pectin out of the fruit, giving a better colour and flavour and helps to prevent crystallisation; lemons are added if the fruit does not have a high acid content; ripe fruit has adequate pectin present; some fruits have more pectin than others, so fruits are often combined to maintain pectin content; sealing prevents the re-entry of micro-organisms; sterilising – to kill bacteria present; pH – the vinegar in chutney lowers the pH which prevents microbial growth;

questionRef: 2023 HL Section C E1 Q1(a)(i) — Deferred sitting
questionText: Outline the historical development of housing styles in Ireland from the nineteenth century to the present day.
stem: ‘It is estimated that Ireland will need an average of 33,000 new homes to be provided each year from 2021 to 2030.’ (www.gov.ie)

rows.contextNote: Five points, each graded 4:2:0. Cover the historical development asked for. “Present day” refers to this 2023 examination. Complete published guidance: Early Nineteenth Century: Rural areas in the early 1800’s, single storey thatched cottage; consisted of two rooms, a kitchen and a bedroom, the walls were constructed from solid stone, the windows were small and the door - usually a half-door, opened into the kitchen; an open turf fire was used for cooking and to provide heat; the thatch was of reeds, straw or hay; some cottages had a room or loft directly under the thatch which was accessed by a ladder, where children slept; wealthy farmers lived in a two-storey, slate roofed houses with up to five bedrooms including a parlour; wealthy landowners lived in a large estate house with servants quarters generally in the basement, etc. Urban areas: Georgian style 2, 3, 4 storey terraced with basements, etc. Suburbs; middle class had small terraced houses, shopkeepers lived over their shops, workers in single storey cottages, etc. Late Nineteenth Century: two-storey, slate-roofed stone buildings; greater variety of building materials available due to improved transportation; more ornate – gothic and tudor styles; stone used; rural – 2 storey houses with slated roofs; urban – moved to suburbs, Georgian houses divided and rented to poorer families, etc. Early Twentieth Century: detached and semidetached; council and housing estates; use of brick with plaster walls; 2 storey as land was expensive; tiles replaced slates; rural electrification (1950’s) and government housing grants changed housing in rural Ireland; the slate roofed bungalow replaced the thatched cottage of the past, etc. Late Twentieth Century: private housing estates used a common design; many different designs for private houses including classical and modern; building regulations improved housing standards; new materials and methods e.g. double-glazing, plastic (pvc) and fibreglass used, etc. Twenty-first century: rural housing developments in small towns and villages; houses of different styles and sizes; renovation of period properties; one off houses architecturally designed; attic conversions, extensions, sunrooms added to houses; outside living space - balconies, decking, patios; improved security – electronic gates, flood lighting; etc. urban areas – housing complexes, which include a variety of town houses and apartments enclosed behind security gates; more houses build on outskirts of towns/cities; high density housing; small living space and outdoor areas; etc.

questionRef: 2023 HL Section C E3 Q3(a)(iii) — Deferred sitting
questionText: Identify and elaborate on the factors that affect an individual’s attitude to work.
stem: ‘Irish job attitudes survey says two-thirds of adults are happy in their jobs.’ (www.rte.ie)

rows.contextNote: Four points, each graded 5:3:0. Complete published 2023 guidance (general examples, not predictions about an individual): Social group: children from higher socio-economic group tend to have higher educational aspirations and long-term goals; they are encouraged and therefore more likely to attain work in desired area; children from lower socio-economic group tend to have fewer educational opportunities and are often less qualified; they may attain employment in low- status positions, with little chance of advancement and little job satisfaction, etc. Education: higher socio-economic group have better qualifications and higher career expectations, they have a more positive experience of work and remain in employment for longer; early school leavers find it difficult to find well-paid long-term employment; etc. Extrinsic satisfaction: based on bonuses associated with work rather than the job itself; repetitive uninteresting work e.g. assembly line – may fail to stimulate so the wage alone may become the focus for satisfaction; satisfaction is derived from spending the money on luxury goods and/or socialising, etc. Intrinsic satisfaction: work gives sense of fulfilment, pleasure and scope for creativity; pride in work; develops self-esteem, confidence, independence; confers status and respect; satisfies psychological and social needs; etc. Work ethic: attitude to work including absenteeism, punctuality, commitment to work and respect for authority, etc. Personal identity: some professions confer status in the community and as a result may link to a positive attitude to work; etc. Working conditions: availability of part time work, job sharing, flexitime and working from home make work life balance easier; atmosphere at work, etc. Social contact: influenced by background; experience; peer pressure; etc.

questionRef: 2023 HL Section C Q4(a)(ii) — Deferred sitting
questionText: Describe the production of cheese. Refer to: • stages of production • packaging • labelling.
stem: ‘In Ireland, 8 in 10 consumers eat cheese in a typical week, with the majority consuming cheese 2-3 times a week.’ (www.bordbia.ie)

rows.contextNote: Six points, each graded 2:1:0. Source correction: the heading says “9 points”, but the detailed allocation is 6 + 2 + 2 points, matching the paper’s 20 marks. Published guidance: a culture of lactic acid bacteria is added to pasteurised milk; lactose (sugar in milk) changes to lactic acid which adds flavour and acts as a preservative; milk is heated to 30°C, rennet is added - contains enzymes rennin which coagulates protein (caseinogen to casein); mixture separates into curds (solids) and whey (liquid); curds are chopped to release more whey, whey is drained off; curds are heated to 35 - 40°c to squeeze out more whey and achieve correct consistency (scalding); curds are cut into blocks and piled on top of each other to complete drainage of whey (cheddaring); the blocks are cut and 2% salt is added for flavour and preservation; salted curds are placed in moulds and pressed; moulds may be sprayed with hot water to form a protective rind; cheese is removed from the mould, date stamped and stored for 3 - 12 months to ripen (mature); cheese is graded; etc.
Two points, each graded 2:0. Published guidance: vacuum packed in polythene zip-lock plastic bag; waxed paper, plastic tubs; aluminium foils; cardboard etc.
Two points, each graded 2:0. Published guidance: type; brand; quantity; nutritional information; date-stamp; storage instructions etc.

questionText: Discuss the rights and responsibilities of a couple within a marriage relationship.

The wording and Acts below are historical examination guidance, not current legal advice. Published 2023 scheme wording: to cohabit/live together and keep each other company; to have sexual relations with each other during the marriage; to show commitment to the marriage and remain faithful and loyal in a monogamous relationship; to provide financial support for dependent spouses and children as set out in the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976; to share joint guardianship of any children born within the marriage, and to meet their children’s physical, moral, emotional, intellectual and social needs. Children may be taken into care if parents do not fulfil this right; to inherit from each other under the Succession Act 1965, e.g., if a spouse dies and there is no will and no children the surviving spouse is entitled to all of the estate; protection under the Domestic Violence Act 1996; under the Family Home Protection Act 1976 etc

Heat and UV inactivation depend on exposure conditions and time/dose; darkness is not a universal requirement. The printed temperatures alone are not a sterilisation procedure. Complete published guidance:

Food: most bacteria are saprophytic and parasitic; etc.

Warmth: Wide temperature range; some are psychrophiles, eg. listeria, some are thermophiles e.g. clostridia, most are mesophiles; temperatures between 70oC – 100oC will destroy most bacteria; temperatures above 121oC are required to destroy bacterial spores; freezing inactivates bacterial growth; etc.

Moisture: is needed for growth in liquid form, thus frozen foods are unsuitable; etc.

Oxygen: most bacteria are aerobic, need oxygen, eg. E-coli; some are anaerobic eg. clostridium botulinum and some are facultative e.g. salmonella; etc.

pH level: bacteria like neutral or slightly acidic conditions, extreme acids or alkaline conditions inhibit growth; etc.

Time: bacteria need time to multiply, they will double every 20 minutes in correct conditions; etc.

Light: bacteria need darkness and are destroyed by UV light; etc.

questionText: Describe the stages in a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) system for making a hot main course dish. Refer to potential hazards and the corresponding control measures that should be implemented.
stem: Temperature control is critical to ensuring food safety for all consumers.

rows.contextNote:
Name stage 1 of your HACCP plan, graded 1:0. All seven published stage examples follow; choose four relevant stages. Source correction: FSAI recommends cooking to a 75°C core or a validated time/temperature equivalent and reheating to at least 70°C, not a general requirement to exceed 100°C. Keep chilled food at 0–5°C and hot-held food above 63°C. Historical examples below are not a complete food-safety procedure. Complete two-page table: Purchase — hazards: Damaged goods; Contamination – bacterial, chemical Pests; Control measures: • Buy food from a reputable shop • Check that raw and cooked foods are stored separately • Check packaging • Check best before and use by dates • Check fridge/freezer/food temperature • Check for signs of pest damage • Use cool bags for transport of perishables etc.

Transportation — hazards: Multiplication of bacteria caused by a rise in temperature; Cross contamination; Damaged packaging; Control measures: • Ensure perishable foods are packed in a cool bag • Pack perishable and non-perishable foods separately • Allow the shortest time possible between purchase & storage • Ensure packaging remains intact etc.

Storage — hazards: Damaged goods Contamination – bacterial, chemical Pests; Multiplication of bacteria; Cross contamination; Control measures: • Cover chilled food and store at 5°C or below • Store frozen food at – 18°C • Check vegetables for mould etc.

Preparation — hazards: Contamination – bacterial, chemical; Multiplication of bacteria; Cross contamination; Control measures: • Foods within date and with quality assurance marks • Hands washed with antibacterial soap before and after handling food; handle food as little as possible; • Colour coded boards to prevent cross contamination; keep all food covered; avoid cross-contamination by ensuring that raw food does not come into contact with cooked food • make sure frozen foods are fully defrosted, defrost in the fridge if possible • Use separate utensils for handling raw and cooked meat; keep perishable foods like salads, coleslaw and quiche in the fridge until needed; keep raw meat separate from cooked meat and ready-to-eat foods like salads • Maintain the fridge temperature below 5°C, this temperature will delay the growth of micro-organisms • Ensure that containers used for storage are absolutely clean • Avoid having foods for too long in danger zone 6 - 63°C etc.

Cooking — hazards: Multiplication of bacteria; Cross contamination; Survival of bacteria; Food poisoning; Control measures: • When cooking poultry always ensure that sufficiently high temperatures 72°C or higher are reached to prevent the risk of food poisoning • Make sure food has been cooked thoroughly, this is particularly important when cooking poultry, pork, minced meat etc.

Serving — hazards: Cross contamination; Growth of surviving bacteria; Control measures: • Clean utensils must be used • Serve cooked food immediately after cooking • Cooked food must be 63°C or higher etc.

Reheating / hot holding — hazards: Multiplication of bacteria; Control measures: • Food must be covered and stored properly before reheating • If reheating food, make sure it reaches temperatures above 100° C • Reheat once only • Cooked foods must be kept at 63°C or higher • Hold cooked food for a maximum of 90 minutes etc.

questionText: Set out details of the findings of a comparative evaluation you have carried out on a food which can be preserved using two different methods of preservation. In your answer refer to: • name of food • suitable methods of preservation • the underlying principle of each method of preservation • risk of food spoilage.
stem: Preserving food to extend its shelf life, whilst ensuring it’s safety and quality, is a central aim of the food industry.

rows.contextNote: The printed tariff names a food but supplies no model food; no example has been invented.

rows.verbatim: the underlying principle of each method
rows.contextNote: Two points for the first chosen method. Complete source guidance: Freezing – removal of warmth and moisture to inactivate enzymes; ice crystals formed so liquid is unavailable to bacteria; on thawing temperature rises, moisture becomes available and bacteria grow again; blanching before freezing inactivates enzymes; colour, flavour and nutritive value maintained if stored correctly; freeze at -25˚C store at -18˚C; repeated defrosting / thawing can encourage microbial growth; freezer burn results in toughening, drying out and discolouration etc. Bottling/canning – sterilisation at high temperatures destroys enzymes and micro-organisms; a vacuum is formed by the lid preventing re-entry of air and micro-organisms; loss of colour, flavour due to high temps; if cans are dented, food could become spoiled due to presence of clostridium botulinium, “blown” cans indicate the presence of bacteria etc. Dehydration – moisture removed and sugar/salt concentration increases, micro-organisms cannot multiply; long shelf life when stored correctly in cool, dry well ventilated area; risk of bacterial contamination when liquid added; pests etc. Chemical – e.g. addition of salt, sugar, alcohol, vinegar, acids, sulphur dioxide, and nitrate; chemical preservatives form a concentrated solution in the food, in an attempt to equalise the concentration water is drawn from the microbial cell and dies; alcohol denatures protein in bacterial cells; acids lower pH to unacceptable level for microbial growth and enzyme activity; micro-organisms cannot survive sugar concentrations above 65%, salt causes microbial cells to become dehydrated by osmosis etc. Irradiation – a defined dose of ionising gamma rays go through the food to sterilise it, to delay ripening, to inhibit or destroy food poisoning bacteria and to prevent sprouting; little change in colour, flavour & texture; food is sterilised – very long shelf life etc. Pasteurisation; UHT; Sterilisation; Freeze-drying etc.

rows.verbatim: the underlying principle of each method
rows.contextNote: Two points for the second chosen method. Complete source guidance: Freezing – removal of warmth and moisture to inactivate enzymes; ice crystals formed so liquid is unavailable to bacteria; on thawing temperature rises, moisture becomes available and bacteria grow again; blanching before freezing inactivates enzymes; colour, flavour and nutritive value maintained if stored correctly; freeze at -25˚C store at -18˚C; repeated defrosting / thawing can encourage microbial growth; freezer burn results in toughening, drying out and discolouration etc. Bottling/canning – sterilisation at high temperatures destroys enzymes and micro-organisms; a vacuum is formed by the lid preventing re-entry of air and micro-organisms; loss of colour, flavour due to high temps; if cans are dented, food could become spoiled due to presence of clostridium botulinium, “blown” cans indicate the presence of bacteria etc. Dehydration – moisture removed and sugar/salt concentration increases, micro-organisms cannot multiply; long shelf life when stored correctly in cool, dry well ventilated area; risk of bacterial contamination when liquid added; pests etc. Chemical – e.g. addition of salt, sugar, alcohol, vinegar, acids, sulphur dioxide, and nitrate; chemical preservatives form a concentrated solution in the food, in an attempt to equalise the concentration water is drawn from the microbial cell and dies; alcohol denatures protein in bacterial cells; acids lower pH to unacceptable level for microbial growth and enzyme activity; micro-organisms cannot survive sugar concentrations above 65%, salt causes microbial cells to become dehydrated by osmosis etc. Irradiation – a defined dose of ionising gamma rays go through the food to sterilise it, to delay ripening, to inhibit or destroy food poisoning bacteria and to prevent sprouting; little change in colour, flavour & texture; food is sterilised – very long shelf life etc. Pasteurisation; UHT; Sterilisation; Freeze-drying etc.

questionText: Explain three principles of design and give an example of the application of each in interior design.
stem: An awareness of the elements and principles of design is essential when creating successful visual compositions.

options: Proportion – this is the relationship between different objects and their size. All objects in a room must be of a size / height that is relative to all other items intended for the room. This must be applied to colours, patterns and textures in the room.
Emphasis – this is where the eye is drawn to an object or a particular area or feature within the room. This is referred to as the room’s focal point e.g. a fireplace in a living room.

Balance – this means that there is harmony between each part of the design of a room. No one room feature or element should dominate the other. There should be an equal amount of colour, pattern and texture that work well together. A well balanced room is aesthetically pleasing.

Rhythm – this is where colours or patterns repeated on different objects draw the room together. It is achieved by linking various objects in a room. This can be done by repeating a different colour in different places or using items of similar style, shape or pattern throughout the room.

questionText: Discuss the adequacy of housing provision in Ireland today.
stem: For most young people, especially single individuals, buying a house is still a far-off prospect given reduced income levels and increasing unemployment.

rows.contextNote: Use distinct relevant points at the source’s printed value. No finer partial-credit ladder is printed. Complete source guidance: Private housing – very high level of home ownership 80% home owners, higher than EU average, government policy has encouraged home ownership e.g. mortgage interest relief, tenant purchase schemes etc. In the recent past (celtic tiger boom) increased economic prosperity, low interest rates, a growing young population created conditions of high demand for home ownership. At its height demand exceeded supply. Huge numbers of houses built. This has now changed. Building industry slowed down considerably. Many houses built and are not selling. Value of property has reduced but market still very slow. Supply currently exceeds demand in some areas. Social housing – provided for people on lower incomes or those who are unable to afford a private house, provided by the local authority mainly or by voluntary or co-operative housing groups. Substantial increase in the number of people on waiting lists; can be waiting for a number of years. Supply does not meet demand. Families, disabled and elderly get priority, single people are disadvantaged. ‘Improvements works’ schemes in lieu of local authority housing scheme etc. Private rental sector - High demand for rented accommodation among young single workers or students; demand mainly in urban areas, availability is limited and sometimes of poor quality. Purpose built housing for students provides rental accommodation but availability is limited. Supply of rental properties has increased significantly in recent years and in some areas supply exceeds demands etc.

questionText: Discuss the influence of each of the following as a contributory factor to poverty in Ireland today: • the economic recession • social policy • the cycle of deprivation in families and geographical areas.

rows.contextNote: Use distinct relevant points at the source’s printed value. No finer partial-credit ladder is printed. Complete source guidance: Economic recession – when economy is weak / in recession unemployment levels rise; world economy / globalisation many jobs lost in manufacturing industry etc.; levels of demand for products and services has fallen so many indigenous companies closed and in debt, little hope for the future. Social Policy – if wages are low there is little incentive for long term unemployed to return to the workforce as they may loose some of their benefits and end up financially less better off. Social policy may perpetrate poverty if the benefits gained leave little incentive to gain employment. Cycle of deprivation and geographical areas – children from lower socio economic groups may not have the same opportunities as those from higher socio economic groups. This may result in unemployment or poorly paid jobs. In turn their children have the same experiences and the cycle continues. Poverty results from lack of education and lack of education can lead to poverty. Unemployment black spots; Industries closing down in areas with few other employment opportunities etc.

questionText: Name one method used to tenderise meat and explain the principle involved.

rows.verbatim: Hanging – animals rested before slaughter to allow glycogen to build up in their muscles. After slaughter muscles stiffen in rigor mortis, making the meat tough. During hanging the glycogen changes to lactic acid, which helps to tenderise the meat. Proteolytic enzymes present in the meat help to break down fibres.
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 6 marks for the complete question, with no per-answer allocation or partial-credit ladder. Check the complete response; no separate answer marks have been inferred.

rows.verbatim: Mechanical breakdown – pounding the meat with a meat hammer or piercing with knives helps to tenderise the meat by breaking down the meat fibres.
Mincing of tougher cuts of meat breaks down the meat fibres.
Tenderisers – sprinkled on meat before cooking these contain proteolytic enzymes which breakdown the meat fibres making them more digestible e.g. papain, bromelin.
Marinating – before cooking soaking or coating meat with a marinade mixture e.g. oil, wine, lemon juice/vinegar and flavourings helps to tenderise the meat.
Slow moist methods of cooking tenderise the meat fibres – e.g. stewing, braising.

stem: The National Dairy Council (NDC) plays a vital role in driving a sustainable dairy industry in Ireland and in educating consumers on the role of dairy in their lifestyles. rows.verbatim: the structure of an amino acid
rows.contextNote: a carbon atom at the centre with 4 bonds: H = hydrogen atom, NH2 = amino group, COOH = carboxyl group, R = varies depending on amino acid.

rows.verbatim: how a peptide bond is formed
rows.contextNote: forms when 2 amino acids join together. The NH2 group (alkaline) of one amino acid reacts with the COOH group (acidic) of another amino acid. The NH2 group loses a hydrogen atom. The COOH group loses an OH group. This results in the loss of a water (H2O) molecule and is called a condensation reaction.

options: Denaturation – unfolding of the protein chain resulting in an irreversible change in shape. This can be caused by Heat – moist heat collagen changes to gelatine tenderising meat, dry heat causes shrinkage and toughening of meat. Acids – lower pH e.g. milk souring bacteria in cheese making, vinegar in marinades to tenderise meat. Enzymes – rennin in stomach coagulates milk Mechanical action – whisking egg whites Salt – increase firmness in cheese
Solubility – insoluble in water except egg white in cold water and collagen in hot water.
Maillard Reaction – reaction between amino acids and carbohydrates resulting in food browning. e.g. toast
Elasticity – some proteins are elastic e.g. gluten
Gel Formation – some can absorb water and form a gel e.g. gelatine used as a setting agent.

questionText: Write an informative account of diabetes. Refer to: • types • symptoms • specific dietary requirements that should be followed in order to manage the condition.
stem: ‘Diabetes affects people from all walks of life, from the very young to the very old and is now considered an epidemic that is exploding across the world.’ (World Health Organisation)

rows.contextNote: Six points across the requested types. Historical scheme guidance: Type 1 - (insulin dependent, juvenile or childhood onset), deficient insulin production and requires daily administration of insulin. Type 2 - (non insulin dependent or adult onset) results from the body’s ineffective use of insulin. Type 2 comprises 90% of people with diabetes and is largely the result of excess body weight and physical inactivity. Previously associated with adults only but now also occurring in children. Gestational - is hyperglycaemia with onset or first recognition during pregnancy.

options: Eat 3 regular meals a day to stabilise blood sugar levels
Reduce sugar intake, use artificial sweetener
Eat a healthy diet of between 3 and 5 servings of fruit and vegetables a day

options: Reflected – rays of light bounce off a shiny surface – glazed ceramic tiles, mirrors, white ceiling.

Diffused – rays are scattered when they pass through translucent substances or hit non reflecting surface e.g. opaque lamp shades.

Dispersed – rays of light that pass through a prism or crystal break down in to their component colours e.g. crystal chandelier.

questionText: Explain each of the following options that couples, who are experiencing relationship difficulties, may consider: • marriage counselling • legal separation • divorce.

Historical 2011 procedure. Source: legal separation e.g. no chance of reconciliation, it is a legally binding contract between spouses, a solicitor will generally draw up the terms of the separation, sets out future rights and responsibilities, partners agree to live apart, arrangements are made regarding the responsibility for the care of dependent children, agree on maintenance for the support of dependent spouse and children, arrangements regarding ownership and occupation of the family home such as mortgage repayments, rights of spouse to inherit from each other, etc.

Historical 2011 procedure. Source: divorce. e.g. couple agree to terminate their marriage legally, application to court for a decree of divorce, solicitor must inform the applicant about counselling, the solicitor must also make the couple aware of legal separation as an alternative, spouses must have lived apart for four of the previous five years, no prospect of reconciliation, adequate provision must be made for spouses and dependent children, court may make additional orders on issues such as child custody and access, property, maintenance, etc.

Legal separation — e.g.it is a legally binding contract, outlines who is responsible for the care and maintenance of the children, inheritance rights, court may make barring and safety orders, etc.

Legal separation — e.g. children might not like being separated from one parent, can become withdrawn as they may feel responsible for the break-up, a drop in living standards or change of home can be emotionally stressful for spouse and children, cannot get married again, etc.
Divorce — e.g. adequate provision is made for spouses and children, can be done on–line to save costs, a decree of divorce gives spouses a right to re-marry, etc.

Divorce — e.g. neither partner can marry until divorce is finalised, it is expensive so spouses may suffer financial loss, spouses may experience a sense of failure, rejection or guilt, they may become lonely, isolated and depressed, they may resort to drink, etc.

questionText: To ensure that food is safe to eat, discuss the importance of each of the following: • food storage • cooking and reheating procedures • kitchen hygiene.
